lessons.title: Due Diligence, Definitive Agreements and Closing the Round

children.text: The term sheet is signed and the founder tells the team the round is done. It is not. Between that signature and money in the bank sit six to twelve weeks of diligence, three or four long legal documents, a list of conditions to be satisfied and a set of filings. Rounds die in this window, and the ones that survive are often reshaped in it. This lesson walks through what happens, what gets checked, and where founders sign away more than they realise.

body.text: Diligence does not create problems, it discovers them. Everything an investor's lawyer will find already exists in your company today. The only choice you have is whether you find it first.

children.text: From Signature to Money: The Sequence

body.title: Term sheet to closing, typically 6 to 12 weeks

events.title: Term sheet signed
events.description: Commercial terms agreed. The exclusivity clause starts running, so your leverage is now on a clock.

events.title: Confirmatory diligence
events.description: Legal, financial, business and technology workstreams run in parallel, usually through external advisers, with a rolling list of questions.

events.title: Definitive agreements drafted and negotiated
events.description: The share subscription agreement, shareholders' agreement and amended Articles are drafted, marked up and argued over, alongside a disclosure letter.

events.title: Conditions precedent
events.description: Things that must be done before money moves: ESOP scheme adopted, IP assignments signed, related-party arrangements cleaned up, approvals passed, valuation report obtained.

events.title: Signing, funding and allotment
events.description: Documents signed, money received in the company's bank account, shares allotted by the board and certificates issued.

events.title: Conditions subsequent and filings
events.description: Statutory filings with the Registrar, and where a foreign investor is involved, reporting under the foreign exchange rules. Lesson 4.4 covers this layer in detail.

body.label: The clock that works against you
body.context: During diligence you cannot talk to other investors and you are still burning cash. Every week of delay strengthens the investor's position. This is why founders prepare the data room before signing the term sheet, not after.

cells: Legal
Incorporation records, cap table, prior rounds, board minutes, contracts, IP, litigation, employment terms
Cap table does not reconcile with filings; freelancer-built IP unassigned; unsigned resolutions
Financial
Revenue recognition, bank reconciliations, GST and TDS, payroll, provident fund, related-party transactions
Revenue booked before delivery; cash sales without trail; unpaid statutory dues
Business
Customer calls, cohort validation, churn, pipeline, pricing, concentration
Customers describe usage very differently from the deck; churn higher than reported
Technology and data
Code ownership, architecture, security practices, personal data handling, third-party licences
Production access held by ex-employees; customer data stored without consent or controls

body.text: Customer reference calls are the stage founders underestimate most. An investor will speak to five or six customers directly, and they will ask open questions: what does this product actually do for you, what would you use instead, would you renew at a higher price. A single customer saying "honestly we barely use it" can undo six weeks of good meetings.

body.title: A data room index you can build before you need it
steps: Corporate: certificate of incorporation, MOA and AOA, all board and shareholder resolutions, statutory registers.
Cap table: current table, share certificates, allotment filings, all prior round documents and convertible instruments.
Financial: audited accounts for the last two years, monthly management accounts, bank statements, the financial model.
Tax and statutory: GST returns, TDS filings, provident fund and professional tax records, income tax returns.
Commercial: top 20 customer contracts, key vendor agreements, standard terms of service.
People: employment agreements, offer letters, the ESOP scheme, grant letters and the option register.
IP: trademark filings, IP assignment agreements for employees and contractors, domain and account ownership records.
Metrics: cohort data, revenue by customer by month, CAC by channel, churn and retention analysis.
Disclosures: pending litigation, notices from any authority, related-party arrangements, anything you would rather not show.

children.text: The Documents That Replace the Term Sheet

cells: Share subscription agreement
The purchase itself: how many shares, at what price, on what conditions
Conditions precedent, representations and warranties, indemnity
Shareholders' agreement
The ongoing relationship: board, reserved matters, transfers, exit, information rights
Whether the term sheet's commercial deal has quietly expanded
Amended Articles of Association
Embeds the key rights into the company's constitution
Terms only in the shareholders' agreement can be harder to enforce against the company
Disclosure letter
Lists exceptions to the warranties you are giving
This document protects you. Under-disclosing is how founders create liability

body.title: Representations, warranties and indemnity, in plain language

children.text: A warranty is a statement of fact you promise is true: the company owns its IP, the accounts are accurate, there is no undisclosed litigation, all statutory dues are paid. If one turns out to be false, the investor can claim compensation under the indemnity.

In Indian venture deals, founders are often asked to give these warranties personally, alongside the company. That matters enormously, because a personal warranty can reach your own assets. Four things to negotiate:
commonly expressed as a percentage of the investment amount, and ideally lower for founders than for the company.
so warranties expire after an agreed time rather than hanging over you indefinitely. Tax and title warranties usually survive longer.
so you warrant what you actually know rather than every fact in a company you did not fully control before this round.
so each founder is responsible for their own share and not automatically for a co-founder's.
And disclose everything. A risk written into the disclosure letter is a risk the investor accepted. The same risk left out is a breach of warranty.

body.title: How much can they claim?
body.prompt: An investor puts ₹30 crore into a company. Founder warranty liability is capped at 25% of the investment amount. A warranty breach later causes the investor a loss of ₹9 crore. What is the maximum the founders can be required to pay, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: 25% × ₹30 crore = ₹7.5 crore, so the claim is limited to that even though the loss was ₹9 crore. Without a cap the exposure would be the full loss, and in some drafts the full investment amount. This is why the cap, the survival period and several liability are worth real negotiating effort.

children.text: Conditions Precedent: The To-Do List Before Money Moves

stats.label: Corporate housekeeping
stats.context: Board and shareholder resolutions, updated statutory records

stats.label: Cleanup items
stats.context: Assignments signed, arrangements ended or disclosed, scheme adopted

stats.label: Valuation report
stats.context: Required for the issue of shares, covered in Lesson 4.4

stats.label: Tranching
stats.context: Later tranches released against agreed milestones, so read those milestones carefully

body.text: Treat conditions precedent as a project with named owners and dates, not a legal formality. Most delays between term sheet and closing are not investor hesitation, they are a founder waiting on a company secretary, a valuer or a signature from an agency in another city. Every week you save here is a week of runway you keep.

body.title: What happens at closing?
body.question: Which of these correctly describes the moment a round actually closes?
options: The term sheet is signed and the investor announces the investment
Diligence is completed with no material findings
Definitive agreements are signed, conditions precedent are satisfied, the money reaches the company's account and the board allots shares
The investor's investment committee approves the deal
body.explanation: A round is closed when the documents are signed, the conditions are met, the funds are received and shares are allotted to the investor. Everything before that, including committee approval and a signed term sheet, is intent. Founders who spend against an unclosed round put the company at real risk.

body.title: Diligence finds a hole
body.scenario: Four weeks into diligence on a ₹35 crore Series A, the investor's accountants flag two issues at Tarang Systems. First, about ₹1.4 crore of the ₹6.2 crore revenue reported for last year came from annual contracts recognised fully at signing rather than across the contract period. Second, provident fund dues for nine months were paid late, with interest still outstanding. The founders did not hide either item, and their auditor had signed off.
body.prompt: How serious is each issue, and how should the founders handle the conversation?
body.modelAnswer:
Issue one is serious but fixable. Recognising annual contracts upfront overstates revenue and, more importantly, changes the growth story the valuation was built on. Restated properly, last year's revenue is closer to ₹4.8 crore to ₹5 crore, and the investor will recalculate the multiple they are paying.
What to do: get ahead of it. Instruct the auditor to restate on a correct basis, produce a bridge showing old and new figures month by month, and send it before the investor's team completes their own version. Then address the real question, which is whether the growth trend survives restatement. If it does, the issue is presentational and the deal usually survives with a repriced valuation. Expect the investor to ask for a reduction, and decide in advance what reduction is acceptable.
Issue two is smaller but must be closed. Late provident fund payments with outstanding interest are a statutory liability and a governance signal. Pay the dues and interest immediately, get a computation from the consultant, disclose the full history in the disclosure letter, and add a condition precedent confirming it is cleared.
How to run the conversation: one written response covering both issues, what happened, what has been fixed, what it costs and what has changed so it cannot recur. Never let the investor's advisers discover the scale of an issue before you have explained it. Founders lose deals for hiding small problems far more often than for having them.

body.title: Before the money moves
body.textWithBlank: The list of things a company must complete before an investor is obliged to fund, such as adopting an ESOP scheme or signing IP assignments, are called conditions ___.
body.explanation: Conditions precedent must be satisfied before closing. Items agreed to be completed after the money arrives are conditions subsequent, and they should be few, specific and time-bound.

columns.label: Term sheet
points: Four or five pages of commercial intent
Mostly non-binding, except exclusivity, confidentiality and costs
Negotiated by the founders and the investor directly

columns.label: Definitive agreements
points: Sixty to two hundred pages, fully binding
Contains warranties, indemnity and enforcement mechanics
Negotiated by lawyers, with founders deciding the commercial trade-offs
Where terms quietly expand beyond what the term sheet said

body.text: Read the definitive agreements against the term sheet clause by clause, or ask your lawyer for a comparison table. Rights that were not in the term sheet regularly appear in the shareholders' agreement, and "that is just standard drafting" is an answer, not a justification. If it was not agreed commercially, it is open for negotiation.

cards.definition: The detailed legal, financial, business and technology review done after a term sheet is signed.
The organised, access-controlled folder of company documents shared with an investor during diligence.
The contract under which the investor buys new shares, setting price, conditions, warranties and indemnity.
The contract governing the ongoing relationship: board, reserved matters, transfers, exit and information rights.
The founders' list of exceptions to the warranties. Disclosing a risk is what stops it becoming a breach.
Items that must be completed before the investor is obliged to release funds.
The maximum amount that can be claimed for a breach of warranty, usually a percentage of the investment.
Releasing the investment in instalments, with later tranches tied to agreed milestones.

points: A signed term sheet is intent. The round closes only when documents are signed, conditions are met, money arrives and shares are allotted.
Expect six to twelve weeks from term sheet to closing, with exclusivity running and cash burning the whole time.
Diligence runs four workstreams: legal, financial, business and technology. Customer reference calls sink more deals than founders expect.
Build the data room before you sign the term sheet, because every week of delay shifts leverage to the investor.
The definitive agreements, not the term sheet, are what bind you. Compare them clause by clause against what was agreed.
Founders often give warranties personally. Negotiate a cap, a survival period, knowledge qualifiers and several rather than joint liability.
Disclose everything in the disclosure letter. A disclosed risk is accepted, an undisclosed one is a breach.
Bring problems to the investor before their advisers find them. Deals die from concealment far more often than from the underlying issue.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not legal, investment or financial advice. Deal documents, warranty positions and diligence scope vary by investor, stage and deal size, and the descriptions here are simplified for teaching. Always engage a qualified lawyer and company secretary before signing definitive agreements. Tarang Systems and all figures are illustrative.
